title: the wheel of rest & the nonbinary of work and rest
content:
on an abundance of rest, rest/work boundaries, and restful ways of working

an inspired analog tool I made

I made a first prototype of this wheel of rest while teaching creative systems.

I cut out a paper circle, divided it into 36 parts, and then wrote down a list of ways to rest. each slice is an activity, color-coded by the type of rest:

green — physical light energy (stretching, yoga, walking, cooking, plants, my dog…)
red — physical high energy (socializing, exploring, exercise, dance)
purple — contemplative/spiritual (meditation, poetry, journaling, spirituality)
light blue — cultural informational (podcasts, nonfiction, audiobooks)
red — cultural immersive (films, TV, fiction)
orange — play (games, crafts)
dark blue — cultural artistic (art, music, film)

the idea is that when I’m wanting to rest — but I don’t know how, I’d look at this wheel of rest and feel an abundance of possibilities. I can turn the wheel to whatever activity or color zone / realm of rest feels most nourishing for me.

I’m sure I’ll make more developed, sophisticated versions of this, but I wanted to share this prototype — and this idea, and think about the role of rest in our work lives.

   

boundaries between rest and work

I was thinking about how to differentiate between the many different types of rest there are — and also, asking myself:

why is it so hard to rest, especially when you work for yourself? aka, why do I always feel like I’m working? could I work less, and still meet all my intentions? what would that picture of “working less” look like? how do we distinguish the boundaries?

what is rest, exactly?
what are the different types of rest?
what is NOT rest?
what is work?
what are the different types of work?
what is NOT work?

in 2020, I wrote that WORK PLAY REST are all just feeling-states; three ways of approaching the same task. you can work as if you’re resting, or playing.

I’m coming back to this same idea.

when I think I’m resting, but I’m working

I spend a lot of time thinking, reflecting, and processing. to most people, this doesn’t look like work — I’m not creating, outputing, sharing, or replying to emails. it’s invisible work. it took me a long time to honor this time as an essential part of my work.

example 1 — journaling in my notebook about future projects and inspired urges might feel “restful” — in that I’m not in active creation mode. most likely, I’m in a liminal, relaxed state. I’m not on any deadlines, and my mind is soft and open. I use journaling (on the couch, with a cup of tea and music) as an excuse to be restful. yes, it’s restful work, but it’s not rest. this is where I get my best ideas.

example 2 — drawing or writing in my notebooks without any pressure to share feels like a small luxury or gift I’m giving to myself, even restful or indulgent — but, I have to remind myself that I’m an artist, first and foremost. this is an essential part of my work. it’s not a luxury, not a hobby, not rest — just because it’s low-effort. it’s work.

   

the nonduality of work & rest

I made this wheel of rest because I want to embody a variety of rest more in my day to day life. rest is the yin (passive) energy, without which I can’t understand the yang (active). therefore: the more I understand what rest is, the more I can understand what my work is. not just by contrast, but by integration.

we are not machines, but we treat our bodies and minds like batteries that get depleted, and need to be recharged with rest.

how would we work differently if we were to treat ourselves as the mysterious beings we are? and if we don’t see our human beings as mysterious — deserving of exploration, experimentation, and curiosity — then, what differentiates us from machines? this premise is exactly why I teach creative systems.

so, what if it’s not about alloting time in your day to rest vs. work — to rest to recharge energy, to work to spend energy. what if both rest and work happened simultaneously, seamlessly, fluidly?

what if resting isn’t a means to an end, but an end in itself?

restful work is work

I think that the bigger invitation here is to reexamine what we define as “work” — not just in our minds, but in our bodies.

is work something that, by definition, requires effort? is work something that necessarily drain energy funds, activates your cortisol levels, while adding funds to your bank account? does work require some level of suffering? is it a form of masochism? (does it mean that activities which isn’t hard, painful, a struggle — not worthy of being considered “work”?)

what if there is a way of working that is easeful, effortless, restful? and even if we find that place, would our brains even accept that yes, this is work, you’re in flow — keep going??

if we haven’t deconditioned ourselves from capitalist/productivity programming, then most likely, a part of our brain shouts at us to stop messing around and get back to work, actual work, the kind that feels like a struggle.

it takes practice to unlearn this kind of response. but even more healing, I think, is when and if we can teach our bodies to learn what work can feel like — when it’s integrated with rest.

rest is embodied deprogramming work

I say this inside the last module of creative systems — that rest is embodied deprogramming work.

rest says to your body: you don’t need to work hard and nonstop, all the time, to prove your value. you don’t need to work to earn your right to existence. your life is worthy, even if you’re not plugged into the matrix. there IS life outside the matrix, and you can create it.

resting is about teaching your body what easefulness in work could feel like. resting makes time feel elastic and malleable, it rearranges the shapes of your work, and, in the spaciousness that emerges, it might reveal a new path forward.

what if resting created more abundance in your life — with less energy, and effort?

it’s terrifying, of course. it feels wrong, like free-fall, but it’s not a trick. if I were to explain the mechanics of how this works, I’d say it has something to do with what happens when you trust yourself so completely, so deeply, so absolutely — that you’re in total alignment with your creative body, and how it wants to move through the world.
